summary: Liz Beavis, writing on the Eight Acres blog (dated Oct 27, 2014), argues the case for raising chickens for meat, noting that small birds are easy to butcher without special equipment and can be processed all at once or a few at a time. She contrasts buying specialist meat chickens, which are bred to grow fast and be culled before crowing, with butchering cross-bred or dual-purpose flock birds, which she prefers because it keeps the farm self-sufficient for chickens and her roosters free-range and taste better. The post acknowledges there are good reasons to keep meat chickens and invites reader comments.
one_line: Liz Beavis's Eight Acres blog post weighs raising dedicated meat chickens against butchering surplus roosters and culls from a self-sufficient flock.
key_facts: Liz Beavis wrote the blog post 'Raising chickens for meat' on Eight Acres, dated Oct 27, 2014.
Chickens are small, so they are very easy to butcher with no specialty equipment required.
Raising chickens for meat allows butchering all at once or a few at a time as needed, which is more flexible than larger animals like beef cattle that can fill several freezers in one go.
For butchering from the flock, Beavis says a dual purpose breed is better because it yields larger hens that also lay well.
Ideally chicks are hatched and raised from the flock and roosters are culled at 4-6 months old.
Meat chickens are bred to grow very quickly and are culled before they start to crow, so they can be kept where roosters are not allowed.
Beavis says meat chickens physically can't survive past 3-4 months old, which makes her uncomfortable.
At Eight Acres, three quarters of the hens were hatched in the incubator from the farm's own eggs.
Beavis says buying meat chicks ties a keeper to the meat chicken industry, which she describes as keeping thousands of barely mobile chickens in barns with no access to the outside world.
Beavis reports that her free-ranging, active roosters have tastier, darker meat than meat chickens bred for large breasts and inactivity.
She has read that free-ranging meat chicken meat is tastier than CAFO meat but not as tasty as heritage breed chicken meat.
Heritage roosters eat more over their 6 month life but provide services including lawn mowing, pest control, fertilising eggs and distributing manure over the paddock.
The post links to a summary about raising meat chickens on the Life at Cobble Hill Farm blog.
The page also lists Eight Acres eBooks, including 'A Beginner's Guide to Backyard Chickens and Chicken Tractors' priced from $12.00.
